h1: Residential Structural Engineer in Perth for Extensions and Second Storeys
heroSub: Adding a floor, a rear extension, an alfresco roof or a granny flat? Get your plans in front of an independent structural engineer who can quote the design, footings and paperwork your building surveyor will ask for.
introHtml:
If you're building up or out, a residential structural engineer in Perth is usually one of the first people your builder or building surveyor asks about. Any change to floor area or height falls outside WA's building-permit exemption for renovations, so a second storey, a rear extension or a granny flat needs a permit, and the permit needs structural documents behind it. Kings Park Structural Co is paid advertising for independent structural engineers: we pass your enquiry to an engineering firm, which quotes you and contracts with you directly.

Perth adds its own wrinkle. A 2025 HIA-commissioned report found WA is the only state where more than half of detached houses are brick, at 68 per cent. In a double-brick house the inner leaf of the external walls, and usually some internal walls, carry the floors, ceilings and roof, so putting a new floor on top is an engineering question before it's a design one. Call (08) 5550 6237 and the engineer who quotes your job can tell you what they need to see first.

features.title: Second storeys on double brick
features.desc: The engineer works out whether the existing walls and footings can take a new floor, and what the design has to change if they can't. Original plans help, so dig them out if you have them.

features.title: Rear extensions
features.desc: New footings, slab and walls designed to sit beside the old house. The drawings detail where the old structure meets the new.

features.title: Alfresco and verandah roofs
features.desc: Beam, post and footing sizes for a roofed alfresco, with wind loads worked out for your site under AS/NZS 1170.2. A roofed patio is not a pergola under the permit exemptions, which trips a lot of people up.

features.title: Footings and slabs to your site class
features.desc: Footing and slab design follows the AS 2870 site class. Sand, usually Class A, is the most common Perth soil, but there are clay sites too, particularly in the Perth Hills.

features.title: Granny flats and ancillary dwellings
features.desc: Slab, footing and frame engineering for a separate small dwelling on your block. Size and setback limits are a planning question, so check those with your council first.

features.title: Paperwork your surveyor can rely on
features.desc: Signed drawings and a technical certificate listing the documents it covers. The building surveyor relies on these when signing the certificate of design compliance.

sections.heading: What the engineer checks before designing an addition
sections.html:
No WA rule sets out a fixed scope for second-storey engineering, so the engineer who quotes your job decides what they need to look at. In practice the questions come back to the same few things: what is holding the house up now, what the new work adds, and what the ground and the wind will do to it. Expect them to ask about:

  • the existing walls, which walls are load-bearing and whether they can carry a new floor (in double brick the answer is rarely obvious from the plans alone)
  • the existing footings and slab, and whether they can take the extra load or need new work alongside them
  • roof and ceiling loads, including what happens when a roof is removed or an alfresco roof is tied into the house
  • the design gust wind speed or wind class for your site, under AS/NZS 1170.2 or AS 4055
  • the AS 2870 site class, which drives footing and slab design for the new work

If the wall that has to go is inside the house, the same thinking applies as on our wall removal engineering page. If there is already cracking, get it looked at before you build on top of it: an independent structural inspection is a separate job and worth doing first.

sections.heading: Drawings and certificates the building surveyor and council need
sections.html:
A house extension goes to your local council, which is the permit authority. You can lodge a certified application (BA1) or, for Class 1a houses and Class 10 structures only, an uncertified application (BA2). A certified application has to include a certificate of design compliance signed by a building surveyor, the plans it specifies, and each technical certificate the surveyor relied on. For an uncertified application the council's own building surveyor makes that call.

The structural engineer's part is the drawings and a signed certificate. You'll hear it called a certificate of structural adequacy (CSA) or structural sufficiency, but that name is not a statutory form in WA and councils use their own versions. The City of Perth form, for example, has the engineer state the AS 2870 site class and the design wind speed and list the documents covered. The City of Rockingham asks for a structural engineer's details, designed and certified by a practising structural engineer, with an uncertified application.

Once the council has everything, the Building Regulations give it 10 business days to decide a certified application and 25 business days for an uncertified one. The clock stops if it asks you for more information. Nobody can promise a permit will be approved. For smaller outdoor structures, see patio, carport and shed certificates.

sections.heading: Typical scope, and what the engineer does not do
sections.html:
Every quote is different, but for an addition the engineer's scope usually covers a look at the existing structure, structural drawings for the new work, footing and slab design, wind calculations, and the certificate your surveyor or council needs. Some engineers will ask for a soil test first. That's done by a geotechnical firm, not the engineer, and it's worth asking who organises it before you accept a quote.

Engineers assess and design. Registered builders build. The engineer does not pour footings, prop walls or put in beams, and this site does not arrange building work of any kind. If your builder is already on board, the engineer normally works from the builder's or designer's drawings and hands back the structural set.

Where you are matters less than people think, but ground does change across the metro area. The Perth Hills and eastern suburbs have more clay than the coastal plain, and in Mandurah and Peel the Pinjarra Plain is clayey alluvium. No source maps a site class to a named suburb, so your engineer will want the class for your actual block.

sections.heading: What it costs and how to get an accurate quote
sections.html:
No Perth engineering firm we checked publishes a price for extension or second-storey engineering, or for footing and slab design. They quote each job, because the price depends on the house, the structure and what the council needs. We won't make up a Perth figure. The structural engineer cost guide sets out what is and isn't published.

The council and state charges are fixed, and they're worked out on the estimated value of the work including GST:

  • building permit: 0.19% of the value for a certified application, or 0.32% for an uncertified one, minimum $121.00 either way
  • Building Services Levy: 0.137% of the value if the work is over $45,000, or $61.65 if it's $45,000 or less
  • Construction Training Fund levy: 0.2% of the value, only where the work is over $100,000

To get a quote that holds, send the engineer your address, any original plans, the builder's or designer's drawings, photos of the walls and ceilings where the work goes, and anything the building surveyor has asked for in writing. Then call (08) 5550 6237.

faq.q: How much does extension or second-storey engineering cost in Perth?
faq.a: No Perth engineering firm publishes a fixed fee, so the engineer quotes after seeing your plans and the house. The only published benchmark is national: Bark's 2026 figures put extension design at about $5,000 across Australia, and the source does not say whether GST is included. That is not a Perth price, so treat it as a rough outside reference only.

faq.q: Can my double-brick house take a second storey?
faq.a: Nobody can tell you that without looking at it. In double brick the inner leaf of the external walls and usually some internal walls carry the floors, ceilings and roof, and 68 per cent of WA detached houses are brick, so this question comes up a lot. The engineer checks the existing walls and footings and tells you what the design would need.

faq.q: How long does the council take to issue a building permit for an extension?
faq.a: Under the Building Regulations the permit authority has 10 business days to decide a certified application and 25 business days for an uncertified one, unless you agree in writing to longer. The clock stops if the council asks for more information. The engineer's drawings and certificate need to be ready before either clock starts.

faq.q: What council and state fees apply to an extension?
faq.a: The building permit is 0.19% of the estimated value for a certified application or 0.32% for an uncertified one, with a minimum of $121.00, and the value includes GST. The Building Services Levy is 0.137% of the value over $45,000, or $61.65 at $45,000 or less. The Construction Training Fund levy of 0.2% only applies where the work is worth more than $100,000.

faq.q: Does the structural engineer need to be registered in WA?
faq.a: Registration of structural building engineers started on 1 July 2024 and a transition period runs until 1 July 2027. After that date, building engineering work by an unregistered person is an offence with a fine of up to $25,000. You can check any engineer on the DEMIRS Building Engineer Register before you sign.
